title: Taste and see (Psalm 34)
hook: O taste and see that the Lord is good

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm thirty-two: when I kept silent, my bones waxed old. Your line was silence was heavy. Did you say the small thing? Day four hundred twenty, the end of week sixty.

You can read a whole cookbook about peaches. Their varieties, their season, the chemistry of their sugars, the best way to tell when one's ripe. You can become an expert. And then someone hands you a real one, warm from the tree, and you bite into it, and the juice runs down your wrist, and in two seconds you know something the whole book couldn't tell you. Some knowledge only comes through the mouth. One psalm takes that ordinary truth and turns it into an invitation, and it's been sung in churches for more than sixteen hundred years at one particular moment.
screen: `A WHOLE BOOK ABOUT PEACHES.` → `THEN A REAL ONE, WARM.` → `SOME KNOWLEDGE COMES BY MOUTH.`

segments.voice: Psalm thirty-four, in the King James Bible: "O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him." Taste first, then see. Not see first, and maybe taste later if the evidence is good enough. The psalm puts experience before understanding. You come to know God's goodness, it says, the way you know a peach: by trying it. And this isn't a psalm of easy times. The heading ties it to a story about David running for his life, pretending to be mad in front of a foreign king so he'd be let go. A detail worth knowing: the heading names the king Abimelech, while the story in the book of Samuel calls him Achish. Scholars have different explanations; the sources don't settle it. Either way, this is a song from someone who escaped by the skin of his teeth. "I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears." And one of its best-known lines: "The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit." Near the brokenhearted. Not the strong. The psalm is also an acrostic: in Hebrew, its verses run roughly through the alphabet, one letter after another, like a child's ABC of trust. And here's where the taste comes in for many Christians. In the fourth century, Cyril of Jerusalem described the newly baptized hearing a singer chant this verse as they came forward to receive communion: taste and see. Many churches still sing it at the Lord's table. And what a week it's been: pleasant places, the heavens declaring, my God my God, whom shall I fear, yalin, the heavy silence, and now, a taste.
screen: `TASTE FIRST, THEN SEE.` · `A SONG OF A NARROW ESCAPE.` · `NIGH UNTO THE BROKEN HEART.` · `SUNG AT COMMUNION SINCE CYRIL.` · then, large: `O TASTE AND SEE THAT THE LORD IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: taste your food slowly. If you have something to eat or drink nearby, a piece of fruit, a cracker, a sip of tea, take it now. If not, save this for your next meal. Settle, and breathe. Put one small bite in your mouth and don't chew yet. Notice the texture, the temperature. Then chew slowly, and notice the flavor arrive, change, and fade. Swallow, and notice the aftertaste. You've just learned something no description could teach you. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Taste and see. Psalm thirty-four's invitation to know God's goodness by experience, like tasting food, and a verse long sung at communion.

Your line: taste and see. Today, eat one meal, or one bite, slowly, without a screen. And that's week sixty: pleasant places, the heavens, my God, light, morning, silence, and a taste. Day four hundred twenty.
screen: `WEEK SIXTY: PLEASANT PLACES · THE HEAVENS · MY GOD · LIGHT · MORNING · SILENCE · TASTE`

howItsDone: Many churches, Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican and others, sing 'O taste and see' during communion, a custom described as early as Cyril of Jerusalem in the fourth century.

what a scholar hears: an acrostic psalm whose heading names Abimelech where 1 Samuel 21 says Achish, chanted at communion in Cyril's Jerusalem.

notes: Week sixty counted as days 414–420; confirm.

Cyril of Jerusalem (or his successor John), Mystagogical Catecheses 5.20, describes the chanter singing 'O taste and see' at communion; authorship is debated. 'More than sixteen hundred years' assumes late fourth century. Confirm.
Psalm 34 is an acrostic with an irregularity (no waw line; an extra pe line at the end); the script says 'roughly'. Confirm.
Abimelech vs Achish: explanations include Abimelech as a dynastic title; the script says sources don't settle it.
